zones.label: Volunteer Mentor
zones.summary: The backbone of most clubs -- unpaid adults who join for the mission.
facts: Joins out of general interest, not necessarily a tech background
Most flexible availability of the three types
Needs the most initial training via onboarding (Chapter 6)

zones.label: Professional Mentor
zones.summary: Deep technical expertise, but the least available time.
facts: Brings real-world software or electronics experience
Can mentor advanced students other mentors cannot
Volunteering competes with a demanding career
Best used for occasional guest sessions or the most advanced track (Chapter 15)

zones.label: Peer Mentor
zones.summary: Older students mentoring younger ones -- less experience, more relatability.
facts: Typically a teenager, often a club alum
Builds the peer mentor's own confidence (Chapter 10 covers recruitment)
Still requires the same background check and code-of-conduct training as an adult mentor
